findings.text: Nothing in the repository tests docs/real-use/findings.md today: the existing release-docs.test.ts cases hold documents to code (commands, files, summary lines), not to a status log. AC-18 adds a test that says which findings rows must still be `deferred` (the GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL/time-limit/MARKETPLACE_TOKEN row, the decideHold/deploy-files row) and which must cite piece 2. A competent reader would build a test that breaks when the next item fixes one of those advisories and updates its row, so the follow-up items would also have to edit this item's test. Simpler: keep the findings rows as prose and check them in review, or check only that the rows cite 2026-11-12-005 and are no longer deferred, not which other rows stay open.
findings.reason: Right that a test fixing which rows stay deferred breaks when a later item answers one. The criterion keeps the test (the security lead's return asked for a record held by a test) but narrows it: the answered rows cite 2026-11-12-005 and are not deferred; the open advisories are named in the file (GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, MARKETPLACE_TOKEN, the time limit) with no assertion on their status, and no assertion on the untouched advisories.

findings.scope: spec Design 1, last bullet; AC-10(b)(c); AC-16; plan Phase 2 step 4
findings.text: Even the spec calls the mask line defence in depth. No other step in the job holds the encoded value, and all of git's output is captured and redacted, so the mask covers no path that the redaction misses. It still costs a fixed ordering ("first statement, before need(VERSION)"), the GITHUB_ACTIONS gating, AC-10(c) (the VERSION-unset case, where no token can leak) and three AC-16 cases. Keeping `::add-mask::` as the platform's standard tool is defensible, but the ordering requirement and AC-10(c) protect nothing and could go.

The architecture section holds code-level detail: the five throw sites listed one by one, the use of `process.stdout.write`, and the literal-string-versus-regex choice. The plan already carries this detail. In the spec, the one rule is enough: every git output is redacted where the runner is wrapped, and that rule is the guarantee.

The user journey holds the whole runbook paragraph: what a second run answers per target (`already published`, `already at`, `latest: moved to`) and the "A bad release" exception. Design 3 then says to copy J-4 "in the words of J-4". A journey should state the outcome (the job is cut, and the person can tell whether distribution started and how to restart it safely); the per-target answers belong in the runbook text and AC-13.

The test looks for exact phrases ("exact match", "no destination from its environment") in ADR 0029 and in CLAUDE.md's Releasing line. That holds wording, not facts that code can check, and any later rewording of either document will break it, even when the meaning is unchanged.

After the reads are deleted, the AC-11 case keeps setting `PUSH_REMOTE` and `PUSH_ORIGIN`, on and off a runner, to prove that a name nothing reads is ignored. The verification grep already shows that scripts/ never reads the names. The `clone`/`ls-remote` target assertion alone covers the requirement.

The spec says as fact that Actions "does not know this encoded form" but gives no source, and the actions/runner secret masker registers base64 value encoders, including shifted alignments; because "x-access-token:" is 15 bytes (a multiple of 3), the token's own base64 appears aligned inside the header's base64, so the runner may already mask most of it; the premise needs a check against the runner's masker or a real run, because it decides whether the mask line (Design 1) is new protection or just a new place where the full credential is printed.
findings.reason: Right, checked on 2026-11-12 against actions/runner src/Sdk/DTLogging/Logging/ValueEncoders.cs: the runner registers base64 of each secret at three byte alignments, and the prefix x-access-token: is 15 bytes, so the base64 of the token sits whole inside the header and the runner already masks it in the log. The Problem is corrected to say so, and the mask line is removed from the design: the redaction inside the script stays, for the step summary (not shown to be masked) and for runs off a runner.

findings.text: On a runner the design adds a line that prints the whole encoded credential to standard output on purpose, and it is hidden only if the runner treats it as a command; the spec names step debug but not the other ways that line can reach the log as plain text: a later `::stop-commands::`, a workflow change that pipes or captures the step's stdout (`| tee`, `$(...)`), or a re-run with "Enable debug logging"; a reader would not see that G-1's one allowed exception is itself an exposure that the redaction does not cover, and no AC or rule in the documents (AC-15) tells a later change to keep push.ts's stdout uncaptured on a runner.
findings.reason: Right: the mask line prints the whole encoded credential on purpose and is safe only while the runner reads that output as a command. With design-1.7-1 it adds no protection, so it is removed, with its ordering rule, the GITHUB_ACTIONS gate and the criteria that held them (AC-10 mask parts, AC-16).

findings.text: "Any change to `gitEnv`" is a non-goal and Design 2 says "`gitEnv` is not changed", but Design 1 has `gitEnv` build its header from `encodedCredential`; that is a change to gitEnv (even if it gives the same output), so the text contradicts itself and should say "no change to its output".

J-4 says a second run for the same tag writes nothing new and only names the "A bad release" exception; it leaves out the runbook's other refusal ("Only the highest release can be repeated: an older tag is refused"), so a hand start after a later tag has been cut is refused, not idempotent; separately, "look again after a minute" has no backing for why one minute is enough to show a late-accepted dispatch.
"ends within five minutes" overstates `timeout-minutes`, which counts only from when the job starts on a runner, not while it waits in the queue; the goal should say "runs for at most five minutes".
"names piece 2" uses a term the spec never defines (Design 4 says "points to the next item"), so the check a test would make on the findings row is unclear.
The ids run out of order (AC-9..12, AC-6, AC-13, AC-18, AC-15, AC-16, AC-17) and the spec explains the retired ids; this makes it harder to map criteria to Design sections.

The spec states no cost or duration (effort, review rounds, and that the change is proved only by the next real tag), and no midway check apart from the ACs; the risks say runner behaviour "is seen only in a real run" but name no point at which someone will look at that run's log and summary for the encoded value.

the rubric's "Proposed architecture" section is titled "Design" and is a list of changes per file, with no named components or data flow (token -> encodedCredential -> gitEnv / redact / tokenMask -> stdout and summary)
the rubric's "Alternatives considered" is not a section of its own: it is an unnumbered third-level heading under Design, beside the numbered subsections 1-4

"none can carry the value. This is the guarantee, and it holds wherever the script runs" claims more than an exact literal match can deliver: git text that splits, wraps or truncates the base64 value gets through `redact`. A reader who takes "guarantee" at its word will not test or fix those cases. The exact-match limit is only stated one bullet later and only about other credential forms.
findings.reason: Right: the redaction is by exact match, so a git text that splits, wraps or truncates the value passes. Design 1 states the limit in the same sentence and no longer calls it a guarantee; ADR 0029 carries the same limit.

findings.text: "a row that names piece 2" uses a term the spec never defines. Design 4 says "points to the next item" and Non-goals says "the next item of the parent concept", so a writer of the findings row or of its doc test cannot tell what text "piece 2" requires.
findings.reason: Right: piece 2 is undefined in the spec. The criterion and Design 4 name the item by what it is (the next item of the parent concept: the client learns of a release and replaces its staged binary) and the row's status text is given: deferred, to the client update item.

findings.text: "Rejected here: those jobs are the backlog's debt point" is jargon that hides the reason. A reader cannot tell why a timeout on the other jobs was turned down, and the feature rubric asks for a stated reason.

"retired when the leads' returns changed their texts" is process jargon. It tells a fresh reader nothing about the feature and could be cut or reduced to "AC-1 to AC-5, AC-7, AC-8 and AC-14 are retired".
"with what the lenses found" and "the security lead's advisory" point to sources the reader cannot find. Neither names a file or finding id.
"the old row" is not defined anywhere in the spec. Which row of `docs/real-use/findings.md` is meant has to be guessed.
"What the deletion buys is stated exactly:" is filler before the fact. The sentence can start at "No named test knob is left in the command."
"which is as good as the token" is informal. "which authenticates as the token does" states the fact.
"Three of them are small" is a subjective size judgement with no measure, and item 1 goes on to describe a leaked write credential.
"None." is followed at once by something the spec says is not known. Either list it as an open question that nothing here depends on, or move it to Risks, where line 106 already covers it.

findings.scope: Non-goals, Design 4, AC-18, Out of scope (lines 24, 74, 95, 115)
findings.text: One deferred topic has three names: "One rule for reading a staged binary's version", "the version rule of a staged binary" and "The version rule for a staged binary". Use one.
"Unchanged when `token` is null, and byte for byte when the value does not occur" leaves out the word that "byte for byte" modifies. It should say "returned byte for byte unchanged".
"the command of `push.ts`" is a stiff construction used again and again. "`push.ts`'s command" or a name defined once would read more easily.

One paragraph holds the given/when/then and then the whole runbook procedure, including how each target behaves on a second run. Splitting the then from the runbook text would make the journey easier to check.
AC-6 sits between AC-12 and AC-13 while the other ids run in order, so a reader scanning by id misses it.
"on a slow day" is informal. "under GitHub API latency we have not measured" says what is not known.

The helper is defined as a runner that "delegates to `run` except for one named git subcommand". That cannot build two of the five cases. The `pull` case needs the first `push` faked as `[rejected]` and then `pull` failing with the header. The second-push case needs the first `push` faked as `[rejected]`, a real `pull`, and only the second `push` failing. A reader who builds the helper as written cannot express either case, and must design a per-call sequence (which call, which answer) that the plan never states.
findings.reason: Right: the runner fake is specified as a sequence: a list of (subcommand, nth call, answer) entries, with every other call delegated to run; the rebase case answers push#1 with [rejected] and pull#1 with the header and code 1; the second-push case answers push#1 with [rejected], lets pull run for real and answers push#2 with the header and code 1.

findings.text: `options()` in release-push.test.ts types `edit` as `(dir: string) => null`, but `editTap` and `editMarketplace` return `PushOptions["edit"]` (`Outcome | null`). Passing them fails `bun run typecheck`, which the plan requires after every phase. The plan does not say to widen the helper's type.

The plan does not say whether the tap and marketplace cases create new bare repositories through the reworked `repository(name, files)` helper or write to the `beforeEach` `other`. It also does not say that `beforeEach`'s two calls change to the record form.

The clone failure prints `Authorization: Basic $ENCODED`, but the plan does not say where `ENCODED` comes from: interpolated by the test into the stub's text, set in the command's environment, or `$GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0`, which the stub receives. The shape of `gitStub(options)` (moved-tag sha, clone fragment, the commit override that copies the manifest for AC-17) is also left to the reader.

findings.scope: Phase 2 step 3(d) and Phase 1 last AC-9 sentence
findings.text: Step 3(d), "a passing run", does not name its target (tap or marketplace). The `token: null` complement does not name which git call's runner quotes the header.

findings.scope: Phase 2 step 5 / Files row for release-commands.test.ts
findings.text: The deletion list names the `repository`, `tagged`, `env` and `git` helpers but not the `IDENTITY` constant or the `run` import, which become unused once those cases go. Lint catches both.

The test requires the number read from `release.yml` followed by " minutes" ("5 minutes"). The plan also says to write the paragraph "in the words of the spec's J-4", and J-4 says "five minutes". A paragraph copied from J-4 fails its own test.

"the two rules, in the Decision paragraph on the token and in Limits" does not say which rule goes where. "The ADR also says writes are tested through `commitAndPush`" does not say whether the test asserts it, or with what string.

The plan gives no status text for the piece 2 row, only that it must contain "piece 2", for example `deferred, to piece 2` as row 66 does. It also gives no source for "what the lenses found" (brief.md line 9 and concepts_brief.md hold it), so the reader writes that row's content without a reference.

The plan calls `commitAndPush(options(editTap(...), …))` and `options(editMarketplace(...))`, but the `options` helper in tests/integration/release-push.test.ts:70-71 types `edit` as `(dir: string) => null`, while both edits return `PushOptions["edit"]`, which is `(dir) => Outcome | null`. tsconfig.json includes `tests`, so `bun run typecheck` fails the phase unless the helper is widened, and the plan does not say to widen it (today's left-alone case gets around it with `as never`, line 150).
findings.reason: Right: the options helper's edit parameter is widened to PushOptions[edit] in the plan, and the as never of the left-alone case goes.

findings.text: The helper is specified as "delegates to `run` except for one named git subcommand, for which it returns code 1", but two of the five sites cannot be reached that way. The rebase site needs the first `push` faked as `[rejected]` and `pull` faked as failing, which is two subcommands. The second-push site needs the first `push` to answer `[rejected]` and the second `push` to fail with the header, which is the same subcommand answered differently by call count. The implementer has to design the fake for these two cases.
findings.reason: Right, same as readiness-1.9-1: the plan specifies the fake by subcommand and call count.

findings.text: The stub's clone prints `Authorization: Basic $ENCODED`, but nothing says where `ENCODED` comes from. The `stub` helper (release-commands.test.ts:36-43) writes a shell script, and push.ts passes the stub only `process.env` plus the gitEnv keys. If `$ENCODED` is left as an unset shell variable, the clone's error carries no value: the post-change case then passes without testing redaction, and stays red before the change only because the mask line is missing. The plan must say to interpolate the computed value into the stub's text in JavaScript, or to read it from `$GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0`.
findings.reason: Right: the stub echoes its own environment, Authorization: Basic followed by the value after the last space of GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0, so the value is the one push.ts built; the test computes the same value in JavaScript for its assertions and asserts first that the unredacted run would contain it (the stub's log records it).

findings.text: The stub's cases list `status --porcelain` but not `status --short` or `diff`, which the dry-run path calls through `must` (push.ts:117-119). With "the same stub", the stub's fallback answers `unexpected git …` with exit 64, so the dry-run case ends in `tap: failed: git status failed…` with exit 1. The case asserts only that the mask line comes first, so it passes while the command's dry run (J-2) is never exercised.
findings.reason: Right: the stub gains status --short and diff cases, and the dry-run case of the command asserts the summary tap: would write and exit 0, so the path is exercised.

findings.text: Deleting the three local-repository cases and the `repository`, `tagged`, `env` and `git` helpers also leaves the `IDENTITY` constant and the `run` import (release-commands.test.ts:14, 361-368) used by nothing, and the plan does not name them for removal. biome flags the unused import and variable.
